records.bodyText:
Dounreay was the UK’s centre of fast reactor research and development between 1955 and 1994 and is now described as Scotland’s largest nuclear clean-up and demolition project. In April 2005 the Nuclear Decommissioning Authority (NDA) took over the ownership of the Dounreay nuclear facility in Caithness on the north coast of Scotland from the United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority (UKAEA).
From April 2023 Dounreay joined the Magnox Division of the NDA. Then in October 2023 Magnox Ltd changed its name to Nuclear Restoration Services (NRS). NRS is responsible for safely decommissioning the first generation nuclear and research sites across the UK. It joins together of the twelve Magnox sites (including Harwell and Winfrith) and Dounreay. It will also, eventually, decommission the seven advanced gas-cooled reactor sites (AGRs), currently managed by EDF, for decommissioning.
Interim End State
Until recently, the decommissioning programme was due to reach its interim end state – the point at which all redundant facilities have been cleared and the resultant radioactive waste is in storage – by 2033, but many thought this target was unrealistic. This date has now been extended to 2070. 
Officially Nuclear Restoration Services hasn’t said what the cost of extending decommissioning work at Dounreay from 2033 to 2070 is expected to be. The cost of the programme was previously said to be about £2.9 billion but costs are expected to jump to almost £8bn. 
The biggest problem is decommissioning the Fuel Cycle Area. The NDA explained at an inaugural Cross Party Group on the Nuclear Industry in the Scottish Parliament that the earlier cost estimate was based on the previous contractor’s plan to basically fill in the Fuel Cycle area with concrete and then chop it up. But we now know that was never going to work. As improved strategies for decommissioning the very complex Fuel Cycle Area are developed, work to dismantle the fast reactors and empty two historic waste disposal and storage facilities will continue.
At the start of Britain’s nuclear programme uranium resources were thought to be scarce. Fast reactors were thought to be the way forward. These reactors, generally fuelled by plutonium, can, at the same time as generating electricity, convert the useless portion of uranium into more plutonium. 
Officially the reason given for the end to Britain’s fast reactor programme was that these reactors proved to be more expensive than expected and by the 1980s uranium was no longer in scarce supply. So, in 1988, Britain decided it would not need fast reactors for the foreseeable future and the programme was cancelled signalling the end for Dounreay.
But Fast Reactors have been a disaster world-wide – economic realities, problems associated with reprocessing (separating plutonium from spent nuclear fuel), concerns over nuclear proliferation, serious technical problems and the risk of catastrophic accident have all come together to stop the development and construction of commercial scale fast breeder reactors. 
One major difficulty with fast reactors is that they use liquid metal as a coolant – usually liquid sodium, which explodes on contact with air. Currently, only one Fast Reactor of commercial scale in the world is operating–the Beloyarsk BN-600 FBR in Russia. India is only intermittently operating its Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR) at Kalpakkam. The French closed down their Superphénix Fast Reactor in 1996 after it had achieved an average capacity factor of less than 7% over eleven years of operation. It had repeated shutdowns, the longest of which lasted four years. Japan’s fast reactor at Monju has been mostly shut since a leak of liquid sodium coolant in 1995. It was reopened in May 2010 but three months later, it was closed again after another accident. In the two decades since the reactor started tests in 1991, it has managed to generate electricity for only one full hour.
The Dounreay Fast Reactor (DFR) first achieved criticality in 1958, and operated until 1977. The Prototype Fast Reactor (PFR) opened in 1974 and closed in 1994. The site also housed a fast reactor reprocessing plant, as well as a research reactor reprocessing plant. Overseas research reactor spent fuel was imported for reprocessing up until 1974 when it stopped because foreign customers were unwilling to take their waste back. Then in 1992 Dounreay re-entered the research reactor spent fuel reprocessing business with spent research reactor fuel imported, mainly from Germany until it was announced in 1998 that Dounreay would not take on any new contracts. Dounreay was also site of a materials test reactor which operated between 1958 and 1969. The Vulcan submarine reactor test facility is also at Dounreay, and is likely to be closed and transferred to NWS for decommissioning.
In 1958 the Scottish Office authorised use of an underground shaft – built to remove spoil during construction of a sub-sea effluent discharge tunnel – as a disposal facility for intermediate level radioactive waste. More than 11,000 disposals took place between 1959 until 1977, when a chemical explosion occurred and the practice ceased. Decommissioning the 65-metre deep shaft is a major challenge. A second facility, the intermediate-level waste silo, also needs to be emptied and its contents made safe. A concrete-lined box built just beneath the surface, it was used to dispose of waste between 1971 and 1998. Contractors started to prepare the ground for a major new plant which will retrieve radioactive waste from the underground shaft and silo in March 2009. 
In 2021, Jacobs and its supporting partners were awarded a 6-year contract to provide a design management team to produce a fully integrated design for the shaft and silo project. This includes assisting with the management of several design and build work packages. While some of the contract will be delivered remotely, Jacobs will also sub-contract work to local companies.
Another major problem is the appearance of radioactive particles in the environment. These small fragments of irradiated nuclear fuel have been found on the seabed off Dounreay, on the Dounreay foreshore and on Sandside Beach west of Dounreay, which is open to the public. One particle was found in 2005 on Dunnet beach east of Dounreay. It will be around 200 years, before the activities of the larger particles, have decayed sufficiently that they can no longer be considered a potential hazard. 
Radioactive particles will keep polluting public beaches for decades to come, and the environment will never be completely cleaned up. It may not even be possible to aim to return the environment to a pristine condition. Despite assurances that the risk is low of a member of the public coming into contact with a particle which is a serious hazard to health.
Since 1983 almost 500 radioactive particles have been found on three local beaches near the Dounreay nuclear facility in Caithness and the Dounreay foreshore. More than 200 of these have been found on the publicly accessible Sandside beach.
Radioactive particles were also discovered on the seabed in 1997. As a result, a fishing ban was implemented to prevent the removal of fish, crustaceans and molluscs in an area of 2km (1.2 mile) radius centred on the disused Dounreay discharge point near where the highest density of particles has been detected. The particles lie in a “plume” on the seabed spread over an area equivalent in size to that of 600 Olympic swimming pools. The fragments are thought to be the source of nuclear material found on nearby beaches. Originating from the reprocessing of nuclear fuel, they were pumped into the sea up to 50 years ago.
Underwater clean-up started in August 2008, targeting a 60-hectare area of seabed where the most hazardous particles are found. By the end of 2012, more than 2200 particles had been removed from the seabed. Of these, 409 were deemed “significant” in terms of their potential health effects. By the end of 2012 all 60 hectares had been covered by the underwater detection and retrieval system. On 12th June 2013 the Caithness Courier reported that there would be no underwater particle retrievals during 2013.
The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA) has decided to give up on its aim of returning the seabed to a “pristine condition”. The Agency has admitted that the contamination will never be completely cleaned up. To do so, it said, could cause “more harm than good”. SEPA opted instead to encourage remediation “as far as is practically achievable” but to abandon any hope of removing all the radioactive pollution from the seabed.
Spent fuel from nuclear reactors, whether at Dounreay, Torness or Hunterston, is not officially defined as “waste” – because it contains “useful” plutonium and unused uranium.
The first of 90 rail shipments of nuclear material from Dounreay in Caithness to Sellafield in Cumbria was made overnight on 16th/17th December 2012. The BBC reported that the journey was understood to have been made under armed escort. The material to be transported falls into two categories.
The first category is around forty-four tonnes of “breeder material”, which was moved in about 40 trainloads over a four or five year period. This material formed the uranium-238 blanket in the Prototype Fast Reactor at Dounreay, so it is not thought to be very radioactive, but there is concern the plutonium formed by the neutron bombardment of the uranium could be a prime target for theft. The NDA estimated that although these transports would cost around £60m, it is a cheaper option than trying to deal with it at Dounreay. This “breeder material” was expected to be reprocessed in the old Magnox reprocessing plant at Sellafield to separate out the plutonium.
The second category is a mixed bag of material called “exotics”. This includes fuel containing unirradiated highly-enriched uranium; unirradiated plutonium and irradiated fuels. This was transported from Dounreay to Sellafield at a later date and will probably take another 50 or 60 journeys over six years and started between 2014/5.
Nuclear engineer, the late John Large, condemned these proposed transports. He said: “We’re talking about bomb-grade material that would be a target for terrorists. It is also fuel from an experimental reactor which will have got broken up and will have been in storage in an uncertain condition. It will be very difficult to inspect it before it is transported and the only safeguard is based on their assumption that they would not encounter an accident with a big enough impact to break open the flask.”
During the period 2014 to 2018 whilst both types of materials were being moved to Sellafield with as many as 15 transports per year.
At 2024, some breeder fuel elements remain within the Dounreay Fast Reactor (DFR) and are still to be removed. According to the NDA’s Business Plan (2024-27) the remaining fuel will be removed and brought to Sellafield over three years and placed in long-term storage, allowing timely decommissioning of the Dounreay site.
The long term plan is fully return the site to its previous condition prior to nuclear operation commencement with a target date of the year 2333.— at Dounreay Nuclear Power Station.

records.bodyText:
In the Gas Turbine, there is a very important system called the Cooling & Sealing Air System. Its role is to protect the internal parts of the turbines from high temperatures, especially the Turbine Blades, Discs, and Combustion Area. 
The Compressor compresses the air, and then a portion of this air is extracted through different stages, especially the Intermediate Stages and High Pressure Stages, according to the design of the turbines, and is directed through special pipes and channels toward the parts that need cooling or insulation.
Typical values for some types of industrial turbines:
- The air temperature extracted from the Compressor can be approximately between 200 and 500°C depending on the extraction stage and operating conditions.
- The percentage of air used for cooling and sealing can be approximately between 10 and 25% of the compressed air flow, depending on the design and Gas Turbine capacity.
- The temperature of the hot gases at the turbine entrance can exceed 1000 to 1500°C in some modern designs.
This air has two main functions:
1- First: Cooling Air passes through special channels inside the Turbine Blades and Discs to reduce their temperature and protect them from damage and deformation due to high heat.
2- Second: Sealing Air is used to maintain
Ipressure differences and prevent the entry or leakage of hot gases toward sensitive areas, especially around the Bearings and inside some gaps.
Because any air flow disruption or blockage in the cooling channels can cause the Blades to heat up, leading to Thermal Stress and accelerating the wear of internal components.

records.bodyText:
The South Clyde Energy Centre will supply thousands of homes with electricity from unrecyclable waste. Drivers travelling on the M8 near Braehead may have wondered what the huge spaceship-like structure next to the motorway is.
Its size and sweeping sloped roof make for an impressive roadside visual, and inside it will become one of the largest Energy from Waste (EfW) facilities in Scotland. The South Clyde Energy Centre is set to begin operations by the end of 2026.
The facility will handle 350,000 tonnes of waste that would otherwise have ended up in a landfill. It comes ahead of the Scottish Government's ban on landfill sites, which is due to come into force in 2028.
Jointly owned by Fortum and Gren Energy, the facility will generate 45 MW of electricity and reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 67 kilotonnes of carbon dioxide per year. This will help power more than 70,000 homes.
Once operational, refuse collected from across the city will be taken to the South Clyde Energy Centre, where it will first be sorted to remove any recyclable material.
Then the waste will be fed into a giant combustion chamber, which boils water to produce steam that spins a turbine generator, creating usable electricity.
The reason for the sloping roof is to accommodate the massive equipment used to create electricity, including the turbines and storage bunker.
The facility will be under strict environmental guidelines set out by the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.
It also has the potential to be retrofitted with Carbon Capture Utilisation and Storage technology in the future.— at Braehead.

Milestone moment at Sanquhar II Wind Farm where they completed the final concrete pour for the last of the project's 44 turbine foundations, with every turbine base delivered on time and on budget.
This achievement is a credit to the hard work and commitment of the site teams, project partners and supply chain, as the wind farm moves one step closer to completion.
David Nicolson, Senior Contracts Manager at Jones Bros Civil Engineering UK, said:
"Completing all 44 turbine foundations on time and on budget is a tremendous achievement and one that everyone involved should be proud of.
Reaching the final concrete pour is a significant milestone for the Sanquhar II Wind Farm project. With 44 turbine foundations now completed, it is testament to the hard work, expertise and collaboration of everyone involved. 
JonesBrothers delivered the civil works package for the project.
Installation of the United Kingdom's first V162-6.2 MW EnVentus turbine at CWP Energy Sanquhar II wind farm marks the most in powerful onshore turbine in the UK to date.
The EnVentus platform was selected for its higher power rating and operational flexibility, helping maximise the strong wind resources of the Dumfries and Galloway region and deliver more renewable energy to local businesses and communities.
This project is part of a 44-turbine extension of the Sanquhar Wind Farm, increasing its total capacity to 308 MW and making it the fourth largest onshore wind farm in the UK.
The EnVentus technology is optimised for the UK's high wind speeds and complex site conditions, as demonstrated by more than 600 MW of projects currently under construction across the country.
Working alongside CWP Energy and local partners, including BMS HEAVY CRANES, FairWind, Collett & Sons Ltd and Jones Bros.— in Sanquhar.

Coalburn 2 Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) 
Coalburn 2 is a 500MW, two-hour duration, lithium ion battery energy storage system (BESS) situated in South Lanarkshire. 
Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) has agreed to divest a 50% ownership stake in Coalburn 2 to funds managed by AIP Management.  The transfer of 50% ownership to AIP will take place once the site is commissioned. The agreement was signed by CIP on behalf of its Copenhagen Infrastructure IV fund. 
Upon being operational, the new project will be among the largest battery storage facilities in Europe, enhancing grid stability and facilitating the integration of renewable energy sources.
In December 2024, CIP took the financial investment decision for Coalburn 2. 
CIP will maintain its leadership in the delivery of Coalburn 2 as it progresses through the current construction phase. 
The project benefits from a ten-year optimisation agreement with SSE and a 15-year capacity market agreement. 
Coalburn 2 is one of three transmission-linked BESS assets co-developed by CIP and Alcemi. These projects are currently under construction by CIP in Scotland. 
Collectively, these assets will have a power capacity of 1.5GW and will be capable of storing and supplying the grid with a total of 3GWh of electricity. This capacity is enough to power more than 4.5 million households for a duration of two hours. 
CIP is also developing an additional 4.5GW of BESS projects in Scotland and England.  
AIP partner investment reinforces their conviction in the UK energy storage market and reflects our strategy of partnering selectively on high-quality, ready-to-build or operational assets.
The investment follows AIP’s recent acquisition of a 2.4GWh portfolio of operational and under construction BESS projects in the UK. 
So far, AIP’s investments boast a total capacity of around 7GW, which together are projected to help prevent the emission of ten million tonnes of greenhouse gases. 
Coalburn 2 site, which once commissioned in 2027 will be one of Europe’s biggest operational BESS projects.  
The delivery of Coalburn 2, alongside CIP’s Coalburn 1 and Devilla projects, will improve the UK’s energy security, enable more low-cost renewables to be delivered, and reduce costs for British consumers through enhanced system flexibility.” 
The grid connection for these projects is via the Coalburn Grid Substation.— in Coalburn, South Lanarkshire.

It is important that anyone who is against the Strathoykel Windfarm development lets the local Creich Community Council know. You can do this by emailing: secretary@ardgayanddistrictcommunitycouncil.org.uk 
I emailed Kerry, who is the secretary and her reply was:
"You are correct numbers are important in terms of objections.
For the CC to submit a representation we need to be sure that we are representing the views of the community.  We have been critiscised previously for submitting objections which some felt were not a fair representation of the communities views.  The bottom line is if the community are not telling us that they want to object we have no basis on which to be objecting as your community council.  We don't need anything formal but if people have concerns then they need to let a member of the CC know.
I hope this makes sense."
Please tell her how you feel about this, so she has some strength of numbers to tale to any salient meetings, It will only take a minute. Thank you.

Great progress continues on the Thorpe Marsh 400 kV BESS project. This site previously contained a coal fired power station consisting of 2 x 550 MW demonstrator units with a variety of different boiler & turbine OEMs and plant layouts
H&MV Engineering is delivering the project as Principal Designer and Principal Contractor, supporting developer @Fidra Energy, backed by @EIG and the UK Government’s National Wealth Fund.
Following site mobilisation and formal handover, the project has now moved fully into the heavy civils phase, with full CDM control transferred to H&MV Engineering on 25 February 2025.
Key works currently underway include:
The civils team are continuing with drainage installation
Cable troughs and fencing works are nearing completion
A.I.S compound works are on-going with electrical fit-out commencing
National Grid User Bay works are advancing at pace
HV Grid Route duct installation complete, cable installation under way
Design development across civil, electrical and grid interfaces continues, nearing completion, with close coordination remains ongoing with NESO, National Grid, and Sungrow.
Health, safety and wellbeing remain at the forefront of this project, with over 130,000 H&MV hours worked with no recorded incidents as works progress across multiple fronts towards delivery on programme.— at Thorpe Marsh Power Station.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
A public inquiry into plans to put 200-metre high wind turbines on one of East Lothian’s historic landscapes heard the county’s most famous son would be ‘turning in his grave’ at the idea.
Scottish Ministers are holding hearings into the plans for the wind farm and battery energy storage site at Newland Hill, near Gifford, after East Lothian Council objected to the proposals.
And as the hearings opened on Monday evening in a packed Gifford village hall, the community had their first chance to voice their views on the plans of the inquiry.
The county’s environmental hero John Muir, who was born in Dunbar and is known as the ‘father’ of America’s national parks which he helped establish in his lifetime, was mentioned by local residents who urged the Scottish Government Reporter to look at the special landscape character of the surrounding Lammermuir Hills and consider the impact of the plans.

Redshaw Substation is a major planned electricity transmission project in South Lanarkshire, Scotland, developed by SP Energy Networks.
Located near the former Red Moss Hotel, approximately 3.5 km southeast of Douglas and adjacent to the B7078 and the existing 400kV Scotland to England interconnector (ZV route).
Granted planning consent by South Lanarkshire Council in October 2025, with completion targeted for the end of 2031.
The substation was increase transmission capacity, improve regional energy security, and integrate approximately 2GW of upcoming renewable energy and battery storage systems to support net-zero targets.
Infrastructure Scope
• 400kV GIS Substation: Gas Insulated Switchgear building (approx. 85m x 45m or 91m x 30m x 12m).
• 132kV GIS Substation: Gas Insulated Switchgear building (approx. 56m x 17.5m x 10.8m).
• Distribution GSP: A small 33kV Grid Supply Point building for ancillary power, lighting, heating, and ventilation.
• Transformers: Four 360MVA supergrid/grid transformers.
• Site Features: Permanent access track from the B7078, internal roads, parking, and a 3m high steel palisade security fence.
Connected Projects
• Glenmuckloch Reinforcement: A double-circuit 400kV overhead line running roughly 23 km from Glenmuckloch to Redshaw.
• Bankend Rig Connection: A 132kV overhead line connection linking Redshaw to the Bankend Rig III Collector substation via the Hagshaw Hill Repowering Phase 3 Wind Farm.
The Redshaw Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) is a major 500 MW energy storage project located near Douglas in South Lanarkshire, Scotland.
Developed by BayWa r.e. in partnership with landowner Douglas and Angus Estates
Located approx. 3 km southeast of Douglas, South Lanarkshire, adjacent to the M74 corridor and the planned Scottish Power Transmission 400kV Redshaw Substation
With a charge/discharge capacity upto 500 MW (consisting of up to 400 storage containers). Granted planning consent by the Scottish Government in August 2025
BESS is designed to support the Grid network by storing excess renewable
energy, balance supply and demand, and support net-zero goals.
A community fund of £50,000 per year, plus local supplier opportunities.
Environmental improvements include woodland creation, peatland restoration, and habitat management for biodiversity net gain.— in Douglas, South Lanarkshire.

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
a new advertorial going out next week in New Times.
Smoke and MIrrors 
Did you know that hype can be used as a verb, or a noun? Here are a couple of definitions and examples of appropriate use.  (verb)"To publicize or promote especially by extravagant, inflated or misleading claims:"  example: Local politicians hype the benefits of offshore wind knowing full well the negative impacts to our communities and environment.  And this: (noun)"swindle, deception, or trick".  example: The offshore wind companies dished out huge helpings of industry hype for years before the central coast leases were issued to confuse the public and impart an impression of professionalism and community concern, when in reality neither was the case.
Offshore wind as a viable energy source has been in the crosshairs locally for several years now and as time goes by the industry proponents' hubris and use of hype has been revealed through astute research by the REACT Alliance and the emergence of recent peer reviewed papers. Worldwide, research has revealed significant environmental impacts (try a 3 degree increase in surface water temps near and downwind from large wind turbine arrays, and significant (20%) downwind surface mixing efficiency reduction ie; upwelling.)
As electrical bills rise, the claims of cost reduction to the end users has been debunked as well and the word "energy poverty" has become a reality in many European countries that have unwisely depended too much on offshore wind's intermittent, unreliable and costly energy profiles. Offshore wind is now being recognized as a costly and unrealistic answer to our more than immediate energy needs. 
As if the economic downsides weren't enough, OSW is found to be highly destructive to the deep ocean and near shore benthic marine ecosystems and as such negatively impacts our fisheries and coastal economies and communities. Additionally, it is proving to be of major concern to our national security as evidenced by Sweden denying 22 new offshore wind projects citing national security concerns around the building of turbine arrays off their coast
It's easy to believe NGOs like the Sierra Club, SLO Climate Coalition and the NRDC, and their pro offshore wind stance without doing your own research; but consider this...would you trust an NGO or politician that is funded by the industry they're promoting?? We sure as hell didn't 4 years ago and still don't! That's why REACT Alliance was founded; to get the public the real information regarding offshore wind so you can make an informed decision. Check out our website....better yet, attend our forum on Novenber 7 from 2-5 at the Botanical Garden. Do your own research and you will find floating offshore wind should never be allowed on the Central Coast.  
We, at REACT,  have coined a new word for those that oppose marine industrialization but support offshore wind...HYPEocrite. DON'T BE ONE! Oppose offshore wind. Speak out for the Oceans. Protect our home!
You have a choice
You have a voice
Mandy Davis

records.title: Wind Energy's Absurd
records.bodyText:
A puzzle from yesterday.
At 5.18 pm Kathryn Porter tweeted what's in the second image - that NESO had requested Emergency Assistance of 700MW.
This was almost immediately followed by another EA for 1200MW; the third image.
At what we estimate to be around 6.15, NESO tweeted this by way of explanation:
Earlier today, NESO was informed that a National Grid Electricity Transmission asset expected to return to service would be delayed.
This reduced network capability during the afternoon period. 
Following assessment of the impact of the delay, NESO issued an initial Emergency Assistance at 16:52 in accordance with established operational procedures.
Emergency Assistance are formal operational tools available to system operators when immediate action is required to maintain system security.
As part of that assistance, NESO initially requested an additional 700MW of imports via the French interconnector before requesting a further 500MW, providing up to 1,200MW of additional support to help maintain system security.
These actions were taken as planned operational measures and in line with established procedures.
Electricity supplies remained secure throughout and there was no interruption to customers.
NESO's control room continuously monitors network conditions and has a range of operational tools available to maintain the secure operation of Great Britain's electricity system. 
Many comments were made to NESO.  The best we can say is that folk took a jaundiced view of the statement, and many, as Kathyn has, referred to the fact that we are in a relatively mild autumn - what is the Winter situation looking like?
David Turver replied to Kathryn:
Could these be related to the new lower inertia limit? Are they trying to prove they can do it by deliberately not dispatching thermal generation, other than  when we get almost to an emergency?
Someone else said:  
Even though we *should* have more gas generation available. 
That's scarcity pricing. Are we running out of gas?
So, NESO gave an answer, belatedly.  Perhaps they were invited to, basically, by Kathryn Porter - who knows?  But as of now, it has not satisfied many people.
